Artificial Intelligence

Ai Agents

Software Engineering

Software Architecture

Engineering Leadership

As coding agents gain repository-wide reach, senior engineers must define not only what should be built, but why it should exist, which invariants must survive, what authority is delegated, and what evidence closes the change.

9 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

AI-assisted development becomes dependable when engineering intent, bounded authority, architectural invariants, verified outcomes, and evidence replace ambiguous instructions.
For the first phase of AI-assisted development, the dominant advice was simple: write a better prompt.
Add context. Define the expected result. Explain the constraints. Include examples. Tell the model what success looks like.
That advice was useful when AI mainly suggested code.
It becomes inadequate when an AI system can inspect a repository, infer architecture, trace dependencies, edit multiple files, run commands, execute tests, and keep adapting after the first approach fails.
The problem is no longer only whether the AI understands the task. The problem is whether the change itself is justified, bounded, and provable.
I reached that conclusion while building a production-oriented AI SaaS system with coding agents involved in the development process. The system had configuration boundaries, tenant isolation, database integration, startup verification, external-service constraints, tests, and tightly controlled execution steps.
What repeatedly surprised me was not that the agent could write code. It was how much freedom a reasonable sentence could quietly imply.

A reasonable instruction can grant unreasonable freedom
Consider a narrow instruction:
Fix the configuration problem and verify that the application starts correctly.
The desired result sounds clear. The authority behind it is not.
· May the agent inspect environment files or secret-bearing configuration?
· May it alter startup code, dependencies, or tests?
· May it connect to the database or another external service?
· May it retry after an unexpected result?
· May it redesign the configuration mechanism if the existing approach appears flawed?
Every one of those actions could be defended as relevant to the objective.
The prompt tells the agent what we want. It does not define the legitimate path to the result.
Now consider a broader task:
Make authentication multi-tenant.
The hard problem is no longer identifying a few files to edit. The real decisions are architectural:
· Where tenant identity is established and which source is authoritative
· Whether isolation is enforced in the API, service layer, database, or all three
· How existing records are migrated
· Which compatibility guarantees must survive
· What happens when tenant context is missing or contradictory
· Which of those decisions the AI may make and which remain human-owned
The nature of the task has changed. The control model must change with it.

Prompt, specification, and engineering warrant
These artifacts solve different problems.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Prompts start the conversation, specifications define the destination, and engineering warrants govern legitimate change.
A prompt communicates intent:
Add multi-tenant authentication.
A specification defines observable requirements:
Every authenticated request must resolve to a verified tenant context. Cross-tenant access must fail. Existing single-tenant clients must continue to function during migration.
An engineering warrant defines legitimate change. It connects:
· Why the change is needed
· Which architectural direction has already been selected
· Which decisions remain open
· Which invariants must survive
· Which trade-offs are acceptable
· What the AI may inspect, modify, and execute
· What is prohibited
· When execution must stop
· How the result will be verified
· What evidence closes the work
A specification defines the destination. An engineering warrant governs the reasoning, authority, and journey.

What a modern engineering warrant contains
Early warrants could focus mainly on operational control: modify these files, run these tests, do not install dependencies, stop after an unexpected failure.
Those controls still matter. But modern coding agents reason across repositories and architectural contexts. A mature warrant must also describe what kind of system should exist after the change.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A modern engineering warrant combines intent, architecture, delegated authority, operational limits, and proof.
1. Engineering intent
The warrant begins with the reason for the change.
Not: Improve authentication.
But: Introduce tenant-scoped authentication so that one application can safely serve multiple independent businesses without allowing identities, records, or operational actions to cross tenant boundaries.
Intent should identify the capability being enabled, the current limitation, the risk being reduced, the people affected, and what is deliberately outside the objective.
Without that context, an agent can implement the words correctly while solving the wrong problem.
2. Settled decisions and open decisions
The warrant should separate decisions already made by the team from decisions the AI may analyse, recommend, or choose.
For example, the team may have already decided that tenant identity must come from a verified account relationship, that client-supplied tenant identifiers are not independently trusted, and that cross-tenant access must fail closed.
The team may still leave open how tenant context is propagated internally, whether row-level security belongs in the first migration, or whether users may initially belong to multiple tenants.
This prevents two opposite failures. If everything is predetermined, the AI cannot contribute useful reasoning. If nothing is predetermined, it may quietly redesign the product.
3. Architectural invariants
For narrow work, a file list may be enough. For cross-cutting changes, invariants matter more.
An invariant states what must remain true regardless of implementation:
· A request without verified tenant context cannot access tenant-owned data.
· One tenant’s records cannot be returned under another tenant’s authority.
· Existing idempotency guarantees remain intact.
· Sensitive values do not appear in logs or test output.
· Failed migrations leave the system recoverable.
· Public behaviour remains compatible unless a breaking change is explicitly approved.
The agent may need to change several files to preserve an invariant. Conversely, restricting it to a guessed file list can produce a local patch that leaves the architecture inconsistent.
4. Assumptions, trade-offs, and delegated design authority
Agents begin from assumptions whether we document them or not. A warrant should make the material ones visible: the approved baseline, working-tree state, identity model, migration framework, test reliability, and environment limits.
It should also state acceptable trade-offs. A small performance cost may be acceptable to strengthen isolation. Temporary duplication may be acceptable during migration. A new infrastructure dependency may not be.
Finally, design authority must be explicit. An agent may be allowed to compare tenant-context propagation approaches and recommend one. It may not be allowed to introduce row-level security, alter identity-provider configuration, or change a public authentication contract without separate approval.
Capability does not determine authority.

Operational authority still matters
Architectural intent does not replace execution boundaries.
An AI may be allowed to propose a better architecture without being allowed to change external infrastructure. It may inspect call paths without being allowed to read credentials. It may generate a migration without being allowed to execute it.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A warrant separates permitted work from prohibited actions, with policy, tooling, review, and audit evidence enforcing the boundary.
A warrant should define both positive and negative scope.
Positive scope identifies what may be inspected, changed, and executed. Negative scope identifies what must not occur: secret access, production connections, unapproved network activity, dependency upgrades, weakened tests, destructive data actions, unrelated refactors, or unapproved retries.
This is not excessive caution. It is recognition that technical access and legitimate authority are different things.

Design verification before implementation
Testing should not be treated as a final cleanup step. The verification plan should follow directly from engineering intent and invariants.
For multi-tenancy, “all tests pass” is not enough. The warrant may require evidence that tenant context resolves deterministically, missing context fails safely, cross-tenant reads and writes are denied, existing clients remain functional during migration, background jobs preserve tenant scope, logs do not disclose another tenant’s information, and idempotency still holds.
It should also distinguish what can be proven locally from what requires independent review or external validation.
A credible closure states what was verified, what remains unproven, and why.

Where does the warrant live?
A framework becomes useful only when teams can put it into practice.
For many teams, the warrant should live beside the work rather than inside a long chat transcript. The medium can vary with the consequence of the change:
· A short WARRANT.md file for a focused repository change
· A structured issue or pull-request template for routine team workflows
· A YAML or JSON document when the warrant must be consumed by tooling
· An architecture decision record linked to the warrant for cross-cutting design changes
· A signed approval record or change ticket for infrastructure, security, migration, or production work
The format matters less than the properties. The warrant should be versioned, tied to an identifiable baseline, reviewable before execution, and closed with evidence.
It should not be buried in conversational history, because the next engineer — or the next agent — needs to understand the authority without reconstructing an entire session.

Know when the warrant becomes invalid
Coding agents are effective partly because they continue solving after obstacles appear. Controlled engineering sometimes requires the opposite.
The warrant becomes invalid when a material assumption fails, the root cause changes, scope expands, a new dependency is required, sensitive output appears, an invariant cannot be preserved, or the authorised environment is insufficient.
Failure creates information. It does not create authority.
A failed attempt may justify a new design discussion. It does not automatically authorize a wider command, another retry, or a broader change.
Rollback and abandonment criteria should be defined where the consequences are material. A plan that explains only how to continue is not a complete engineering plan.

Close with evidence, not confidence
A consequential AI-assisted change should not close with “Done.” Nor is a clean diff sufficient.
The final patch may not reveal commands executed, external systems contacted, sensitive output encountered, temporary changes later restored, failed approaches, assumptions made, or architectural decisions introduced.
The closure record should state:
· What changed and why
· Which architecture or approach was selected
· Which alternatives were considered
· How invariants were preserved
· Which assumptions were verified
· Which tests and checks were executed
· Which prohibited actions did not occur
· What remains uncertain
· Whether the warrant completed, failed, or became invalid
The engineering artifact is broader than the patch: patch + rationale + verification evidence + authorization closure.
